steps.title: Sign in
steps.sees: One sign-in panel on the left — Research Intelligence, a field for an email or username, a field for a password, and a line saying access is restricted to authorized accounts. The right half of the screen is a dark panel carrying the product's radar motif; there is nothing to act on there.
steps.does: Signs in with the work account; nothing else on the page asks for input.
steps.decides: Nothing to weigh here — the two minutes start on the other side.

expect: Research Intelligence is an internal tool. Access is restricted to authorized accounts.

steps.title: Today
steps.sees: Today, 30 August, in the Hybrid Computing workspace: 45 papers screened against the focus fields, 21 cleared the signal bar, 21 carried into the briefing. Underneath, a short brief names HybridGen at signal 76 as the leader, with SolidGPT and “Bridging the Linear-Quadratic Gap” behind it, over a line saying it was assembled automatically from this run.
steps.does: Reads the three counts and the brief, and leaves the sort controls under The papers untouched.
steps.decides: One overnight run with one candidate worth naming aloud — worth thirty more seconds before the meeting.

expect: HybridGen: Efficient LLM Generative Inference via CPU-GPU Hybrid Computing

steps.title: Open the briefing
steps.sees: The edition for Sunday, 30 August, headed HybridGen: the same three counts, the brief in full, and 21 papers ranked by signal — HybridGen at 76.4 ahead of SolidGPT at 64 and the supply-chain paper at 56.
steps.does: Skims the top of the ranked list — the first two cards in full, each with its screening decision, source, date and readiness level; the third is cut at the fold, its score, decision, source and date in view and its headline cut off at the bottom of the screen.
steps.decides: The gap between first and second is wide enough that the day has one story, not three.

steps.title: Glance at the top paper
steps.sees: HybridGen's own page: full text passed, from arXiv, dated 30 August, a signal score of 76.4, and a line stating what the score is made of and what would move it. The dimensions start directly beneath, opening at readiness level (TRL) 4 of 9 — development — with the reasoning beginning in plain sentences and running on past the edge of the frame.
steps.does: Reads the number and the first stretch of reasoning, and stops there rather than scrolling into the evidence quotes and the abstract.
steps.decides: Solid enough to carry into the meeting as a single sentence, with the detail left to the platform team.

expect: HybridGen: Efficient LLM Generative Inference via CPU-GPU Hybrid Computing

caveats: The replay snapshot is frozen at one completed run, so "today" is always 30 August 2026 and the counts (45 screened, 21 included, 21 in the briefing) never change between captures.

The greeting on the Today screen is fixed to "Good morning" and carries the signed-in account's first name — "admin" on the replay — so it will read differently on production. Keep it out of frame-critical assertions.

The brief is composed from the run's own numbers and titles, not written prose. The Today screen says so directly — it stamps the brief "Assembled automatically from this run." The briefing edition carries the same brief without that stamp, so the walkthrough must not claim the line appears on both, and the step 3 frame does not show it. Worth raising separately: the briefing edition is the surface the executive actually reads, so the stamp arguably belongs there too.
The Today screen streams its funnel, brief and paper list in after the header, so a capture that waits only for the address will photograph skeletons. Every step here waits for real text.
The session opens on whichever workspace it last remembered; without Hybrid Computing selected, the counts, the brief and the top paper all belong to a different corpus.
No step in this journey writes anything, so the replay's refusal of writes never fires — though the paper screen's question box is visible in an uncropped step 4 frame and would be refused if used.

Step 4's still is cropped to the reading column — the score and the opening dimension — which is exactly what the step is about. The Schwarz-fit reasoning the executive would most want sits further down that same column, and is in neither the crop nor the unscrolled screen.

On the briefing edition the third paper sits on the fold: its score, screening decision and headline are in frame, its readiness level and author line are not. The copy claims only what the frame shows.

The paper page's score card puts its own breakdown on screen — the contributing parts and their multipliers. The frame is fine as captured, but the walkthrough page should present the score as one number with a stated basis and not transcribe that arithmetic.

Beside the reasoning sits a panel labelled Profile. Its chart is vertically centred in a card as tall as the reasoning column next to it, so on an executive-height screen the panel's visible body is empty from top to bottom. Nothing is missing — the chart is simply much further down — but the full screen reads as a broken panel, so this step's still is cropped just below the opening of the reasoning, where the Profile card is cut by the frame edge in the same breath as the sentence beside it.

The paper screen keeps a single-paper question box fixed to the right. It is empty until someone types, so in a still it reads as a large blank column, and it stays in place at any scroll position; this step's frame is cropped to exclude it. It is also the one write affordance on an otherwise read-only journey.

The clip for step 3 cuts from the moment the action begins, so its first frame — and therefore its poster image — is the Today screen, not the briefing. Use the step's own still beside the clip, or caption the clip as the move between the two screens rather than as the destination. The last half-second also already carries the next step's highlight ring on the top paper card.

Several headings are stored in sentence case and shown in capitals — "Today in brief", "In brief", "The papers", "Signal score", "Dimensions", and the briefing date "Sunday, 30 August 2026". The expected strings match the stored text, not the capitals a reader sees, so any check that asserts against rendered text will report false failures on them.

notes: 4/4 steps reproduced after one repair round (step 4 reframed to the reading column via a capture region); all expected strings present; clip is a real transition. The step 4 frame shows the score ledger as the app renders it; captions treat the score as one number.

steps.title: What was screened out, and why
steps.sees: The run behind the 30 August edition: 45 screened, 21 included, 21 in the briefing, then a table of everything that did not pass, with a written reason against each title.
steps.does: Reads the reasons down the column — the four in view are all papers that use the word hybrid about something other than computing hardware: a numerical method, a GUI agent, an encryption scheme.
steps.decides: The screen is holding the line it was set to hold, and nearly every exclusion is plainly off-topic. The exception is an on-topic overview cut for being descriptive rather than empirical, one row further down the table, and that one is worth reopening.

steps.title: A second look at one rejection
steps.sees: The rejected HPC-QC overview at the top of its page: Rejected against the title, no signal score — Not scored yet — a dash in all five dimensions, and a screening note saying the paper surveys the field without offering new architectures, benchmarks or performance evaluations.
steps.does: Narrows the corpus to Rejected, finds the overview by name and opens it to read the screening note, with the abstract below it on the same page.
steps.decides: The exclusion holds — a survey is not a signal — and the reason is specific enough to trust, so the rest of the rejected tail can be left alone today.

expect: Interfacing Quantum Computing Systems with High-Performance Computing Systems: An Overview

caveats: The snapshot holds one completed run, dated 30 August 2026, so every paper in Hybrid Computing carries the same ingest date and the Ingested time windows separate nothing.

This workspace has no borderline or pending papers. The 45 split into 21 that passed full-text screening, 23 rejected and 1 withdrawn, so the second look in step 7 is at a rejected paper rather than a borderline one.

Papers that did not pass screening are never scored: no signal score, and a dash in every dimension. Widening the screening filter therefore changes the counts and the filters shown but leaves the top of a scored ranking untouched — steps 1 and 3 open on the same three papers in the same order.

The log’s exclusion rows are plain table rows, not links, so step 7 returns to the corpus and filters to Rejected rather than clicking through from the log.

Paging forward leaves the list scrolled to the foot, so step 5 scrolls back to the page heading before the shutter. Its shot therefore shows the head of page two and not the pager, and the caption claims no page count because none is in frame.

journeys.goal: A protected hour with one paper: understand the score, read the evidence, interrogate the full text.

fixtures.question: What hardware setup did the authors use, and what speed-up do they report?

steps.title: The scorecard
steps.sees: One paper on one page: HybridGen: Efficient LLM Generative Inference via CPU-GPU Hybrid Computing, an arXiv preprint from 30 August 2026 that passed full-text screening, scored 76.4. Under the score sit five scored dimensions with their reasoning, the screening decision, the abstract and the archived PDF.
steps.does: Reads the whole record once, top to bottom, without opening or clicking anything.
steps.decides: Worth the hour — every number on the page has words attached to it, so there is something to argue with rather than a verdict to accept.

expect: HybridGen: Efficient LLM Generative Inference via CPU-GPU Hybrid Computing

steps.title: What the score is made of
steps.sees: The 76.4 taken apart on one bar: a fit share, a smaller novelty share, and a readiness bonus this paper does not earn, over three values that can be moved in place — readiness level (TRL) 4, fit 82, novelty 68.
steps.does: Opens the 26 further recorded values behind the number: the rigour, novelty and significance bands, an evidence-gap figure, an impact-reach note, and the passage quoted from the paper.
steps.decides: The score is legible rather than opaque — readiness is what is holding it back, and readiness 4 is the right call for a lab prototype, so 76.4 stands.

expect: What the score is made of — and what would move it.

steps.title: Dimensions, rationale and profile
steps.sees: Three of the five dimensions in view — significance 72, Schwarz Fit 82, rigour 82, each at 90% confidence and each followed by a paragraph of reasoning. Two of the three lean on the same measured result, a 1.41x–3.2x speed-up; the third argues from the breadth of the testing instead — 11 model sizes, 3 hardware platforms. The profile chart alongside names all five axes at once.
steps.does: Scrolls into the rationales and reads them against one another, checking whether the same claim is doing the work in every dimension.
steps.decides: The profile is lopsided in a way that makes sense — strong on fit and rigour, thin on readiness — and the reasoning leans on one measured result, which is the thing to test next.

steps.title: Screening, abstract and files
steps.sees: The screening decision in full — passed full-text screening, on the grounds that the paper defines a complete architecture and evaluates it across the A100, H100 and RTX 5090, and the OPT, Llama and Qwen families — then the abstract, and the stored PDF, held in the research archive but not yet downloadable.
steps.does: Reads the abstract last, against the rationales already read, and notes that the paper is public on arXiv.
steps.decides: Screening reason and abstract say the same thing, so the open questions are about the experiment itself, not about the summary.

expect: Stored in the research archive — download is not yet available.

steps.title: Ask this paper
steps.sees: The Ask console already pointed at HybridGen — the paper named at the head of the console beside its score of 76, and named again inside the question box — with one rule stated plainly: every answer is read from a single paper’s full text. The history beside it is empty.
steps.does: Follows the Ask panel on the paper page, which carries the paper across to the full Ask screen, then types the question the hour has been building to — what hardware setup did the authors use, and what speed-up do they report — without sending it yet.
steps.decides: The claim worth testing is the speed-up, and it is only worth repeating once the hardware it was measured on is named.

steps.title: The answer, with citations
steps.sees: The question at the head of the transcript, and under it the answer read out of the paper’s full text: a hardware section naming Intel Xeon processors with NVIDIA A100, H100 and RTX 5090 cards over tiered host memory and a CXL memory expansion, then a speed-up section giving 1.41x to 3.2x against six baselines, measured over three model families and eleven model sizes. At the foot of the answer sits the one source it points back to — the paper itself, named and carrying its score of 76.
steps.does: Sends the question and watches the answer arrive: first a reading note counting the seconds while the paper is read, then the answer building under it. Finishes at the foot, on what the answer points back to rather than on the prose.
steps.decides: The hardware is named and the speed-up is attributed to a stated baseline, so the figure is usable as it stands; the answer cites the paper rather than a page, so the exact figures are confirmed in the paper itself.
